k-1.x_notes: Strengths: the {1,2} classification is checked and correct throughout (wins at 1,2,4,5; take 1 or 2 to reach a multiple of 3; partner wins at 3,6,9,12,15). It uses kid-friendly large type and every pile is drawn as counters, including the 1-15 tower chart. Problem 4 (play a grown-up with 20 and choose who starts) is concrete and fun. It changes the rule twice ({1,2,3} has losers at multiples of 4; {1,3} is decided by parity), and the two-row game ends on mirroring plus a 2-vs-3 first-player case. Response modes (stars, crossing out, 1st/2nd chips) suit pre-readers. Weaknesses: only 7 problems, and four of them have the same shape (classify a set of drawn piles), so less variety and less depth. Nothing tests greedy play or the take-last-loses version. 'Tell how you win' has no recording space (it can be done orally). Problem 1 is thin.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: 10 problems with real variety, all checked correct. It defines 'trap'. Problem 5 (Ben always takes 2) checks the greedy move: Ben wins at 5, 8 and 11 only. Problem 6 lists every way a 4- or 5-counter game can go (5 and 8 ways, and there is enough rows). Problem 7 is the {1,2,3} traps, Problem 8 is the two-pile game including (1,4), a second-player win with unequal piles, and Problem 9 asks for a mirroring strategy. Problem 10 is take-last-loses (traps at 1,4,7,...). It will not end early and is not dumbed down. Weaknesses: small serif type and tiny pile labels on dense pages. Problems 1-3 split one question into short pieces. Three of the 1-20 trap grids are bare numbers, which is less concrete than drawn counters for kindergartners, though real counters make up for it.
k-1.reason: Y gives the K-1 group more and more varied mathematics (testing the greedy move, listing every game, take-last-loses, an unequal two-pile second-player win), which matches the organizer's complaint that K-1 pages are too thin. X is cleaner and more concrete but repeats one task shape.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: clear, readable large type and low reading load. The progression is a {1,2} table, then large piles with first moves and a why, then the {1,3,4} table (losers at 2,7,9,14,16), then five short claims to judge. Those claims are all correct and well chosen: Mia wrong, Leo right, Zoe wrong, Sam right, and Ana's greedy claim wrong. Then come large piles (30 and 100 second-player wins, 50 a first-player win), two rows including (3,6) and (1,4) as unequal second-player wins, and four rules at 35 (1st, 1st, 2nd, 2nd), which makes children rebuild each pattern. Good room to write. Weaknesses: tables record only 1st/2nd, not winning moves. Problem 7 gives no workspace for building the four patterns. 'Explain' is attached to several problems.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: all correct. The claims problems hit the outline directly. Lee's take-the-rest-of-3 strategy is right and Mo is wrong. Jo is right, and the page asks her to answer every reply all the way to the end. Kai takes 4 greedily and is wrong. The {1,3,4} table records winning moves. It adds {1,3,5} with a parity explanation, a two-pile set including (4,1) as an unequal second-player win, and a creative last problem: invent a rule whose losers are the multiples of 5, then a second one (for example {1,2,3,4,6}). Weaknesses: dense serif text, so third graders must read long paragraphs (Problem 3 is six lines). The claims about the new rule come before the table, which may stall some children. The first table starts at 5.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are correct and well developed. X gets the same ideas (testing claims against every reply, greedy failing, changing rules) onto the page with much less reading and cleaner workspace for third graders. Y's invent-a-rule problem is a strong extra but does not outweigh its heavier text.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: excellent progression. It starts at an accessible level with {1,2} and {1,2,3} tables, then explains the strategy at 100, extends {1,3,4} to 30, and asks why the pattern repeats (100 is a second-player win, 1000 a first-player win). Next it contrasts three rules ({1,3,5} even, {1,4} 0 or 2 mod 5, {1,4,5} 0 or 2 mod 8). A very good problem asks which extra number changes the {1,2} pattern (only 6, since 4, 5 and 7 are not multiples of 3). An inverse-design problem includes a correct impossibility: 2 can never be a losing pile when you may take 2. It ends with well-made two-pile grids for {1,2} and {1,3,4}. Weaknesses: Problem 1 is somewhat routine for this band. Problem 7(d) depends on whether a rule must be a finite list (impossible if finite, possible with 'anything but 3'), which is unstated, though the organizer could use that in discussion. Greedy play is not targeted head-on.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: starts at level with {1,3,4} to 24, recording winning moves. Large piles are correct (100 losing, 1000 take 4, 2026 take 1 or 3). It contrasts four rules. The greedy problem (Dana) is correct: greedy works only in {1,3,5}, and the losing piles are 4 in {1,2}, 5 in {1,3,4} and 8 in {1,4}. Also correct: the why-it-repeats problem, finding every rule within {1,...,6} whose losers are the multiples of 4 (the four sets {1,2,3} plus any of 5 and 6) with a proof that the list is complete, and take-last-loses (the pattern shifts by one, for example to 1 or 3 mod 7). The two-pile grids are correct; the {1,3,4} unequal pairs are (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7) and (4,6). Weaknesses: dense small serif text. Problem 8's equal-piles question is easy for this band.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are mathematically rich, correct and well sequenced, with comparable depth (X's which-number-changes-the-pattern and impossibility problems against Y's greedy, complete-classification and take-last-loses problems); I would be equally happy with either.

overall.reason: The packets are close. Both are correct, well sequenced and free of filler, and X is consistently more readable and kid-friendly in layout. Y edges ahead because its K-1 pages, the band the organizer worries about most, are richer and more varied, and it targets the outline's points about greedy play and changing rules across all bands. X's advantage in 2-3 readability is small.
